newsitem.title: UK: Spurred by EMU, Europe set to cut deficits further.
newsitem.headline: Spurred by EMU, Europe set to cut deficits further.

text.p: Spurred by the race to make the grade for the European single currency, most European countries will slash their budget deficits even further in 1997, according to a Reuters study of official forecasts in Europe on Friday.
At least nine, and possibly more, of 13 countries examined plan lower deficits. Actual funding needs are mixed due to issues such as redemptions that need to be refunded in 1997.

"We're seeing fiscal tightening across the board in Europe," said David Brickman, European economist at Yamaichi International in London. "It's the struggle for EMU that is forcing countries (to slash their deficits)."
Under European economic and monetary union (EMU), member countries' public deficits must be no more than three percent of their gross domestic product (GDP).
Brickman said the average in the European Union was around five percent only a few years ago so, countries are scrambling to make the grade.
While the methods and validity of deficit cuts have been a matter of debate in financial markets, official data show the trend is clear.
Countries forecasting lower net public deficits in 1997 than 1996 include Belgium, Britain, Denmark, France, Germany, Finland, Ireland, Italy and Spain.
Complete official figures were not available for the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden. But the fiscally sound Netherlands is considered a shoo-in for EMU.
And Switzerland does not aspire to join EMU. Nonetheless, there is a high degree of scepticism in markets about how dependable the official numbers are.
"We've been dismayed by the supine official forecasts," said Paul Horne, chief international economist at Smith Barney in Paris.

Noting numbers from the European Commission and the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development, as well as from the European countries themselves, Horne said official data disguise the true situation in countries such as Italy.
He said his bank's model showed Italy had a deficit of closer to seven percent of GDP than the three percent target.
Horne said there had been an "incremental virtue" in the past few years of deficit cutting, although it was now getting to crunch time.
"Over the past two to three years of deficit cutting, they are now coming up against the problem of problems -- this is a jobless recovery," he said.
As a result, nations would need to cut programs like social security and artifical job protection schemes for more savings.
Among the study's findings, Spain, Italy and Denmark stood out as those making some of the deepest cuts.

Spain has forecast a 2.856 trillion peseta ($20 billion) deficit in 1997 against 4.727 trillion in 1996. Italy predicts a 61 trillion lire ($36.7 billion) public sector borrowing requirment (PSBR) versus 104 trillion last year. And Denmark has lopped its expected deficit to 4.6 billion crowns ($715.3 million) from 22.4 billion.
Britain, which remains undecided about whether to commit to EMU, is nevertheless on the deficit-paring bandwagon as well.

It expects public sector borrowing requirement in the year to March 31, 1998 to fall to 19.2 billion sterling ($31 billion) from an expected 26.4 billion in the current fiscal year. ($ = 1663 Italian Lire) ($ = 6.431 Danish Crowns) ($ = 0.619 British Pounds Sterling) ($ = 142.6 Spanish Pesetas)
